answer:
**Short answer:** it depends on what you measure. Where a paper measures it, a sliding window costs almost nothing on short-range quality (perplexity, short contexts). It can cost a lot on long-context retrieval. How much depends on how many layers keep full attention, which layers they are, and whether the model was trained with the window from the start. Only GLM-5 measures the long-context cost directly. Mistral asserts there's no cost, Gemma 3 measures perplexity only, and Phi-4 drops the window without saying why.

## Mistral 7B: claims no cost, shows no evidence

- Every layer uses a 4096-token window. Because layers stack, information can travel up to 4096 × layers, a "theoretical attention span" of about 131K tokens ([p. 2, §2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=section.2&page=2)).
- The paper says the rolling-buffer cache cuts cache memory 8× at 32k tokens "without impacting the model quality" ([p. 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?page=2&search=without%20impacting%20the%20model%20quality)). It reports no ablation of the window, GQA or the data, so this rests on assertion alone. Its benchmarks are all short-context, so the strong results there (beating Llama 2 13B) say nothing about the window's long-range cost.

## Gemma 3: no measurable perplexity cost, on small models

- The design puts 5 local layers with a 1024-token window before each global layer ([p. 1](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.1&page=1), [p. 2, §2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.2&page=2)). The aim is to shrink the KV cache.
- **Ratio:** going from 1:1 (Gemma 2) up to 7:1 local:global has "minimal impact on perplexity" ([p. 6, Fig. 3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.3&page=6)).
- **Window size:** "the sliding window can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity". This was tested on two 2B models, at 1:1 and 3:1 ([p. 7, Fig. 4](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.4&page=7)).
- **Memory gain:** with global attention only, the KV cache adds about 60% on top of the model's own memory. With 1:3 and a 1024 window it adds under 15%, at a 32k context ([p. 7, Fig. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.5&page=7)).
- **Limits:** the evidence is validation perplexity on text-only 2B models, shown only as figures with no numbers in the text. Nothing tests long-context retrieval against a full-attention baseline. The long-context plot shows the models working up to 128K and degrading quickly beyond it, but that tests RoPE rescaling, not the window ([p. 7, Fig. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.7&page=7)).

## Phi-4: drops the window, gives no reason

- Phi-4 uses "full attention over the 4K context length, rather than a 2K sliding window used in phi-3-medium" ([p. 7, §3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Phi-4%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.3&page=7)). There is no ablation and no stated reason, so it tells you about a design choice, not about quality.

## GLM-5: the only direct test, and the cost is real

This test fits a window onto a GLM-9B that was trained with full attention, with half the layers windowed (4096 tokens), and scores it on long-context tasks ([p. 6, §2.1.2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=subsubsection.2.1.2&page=6)).

**RULER, with no extra training** ([p. 7, Table 4](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=table.4&page=7)):

| | 4K | 32K | 128K |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | 95.19 | 91.09 | 75.28 |
| Windows on alternating layers | 94.87 | 12.61 | 6.51 |
| Windows on layers chosen by search | 95.78 | 82.52 | 53.95 |

The search is a beam search over which layers to window, scored on RULER at 16K. Its result holds up at other lengths ([p. 6](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?page=6&search=significantly%20outperforms%20the%20fixed%20interleaved)).

**After 190B tokens of training at 64K, change from full attention at 128K** ([p. 7, Table 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=table.5&page=7)):

- Alternating layers: RULER −30.35, MRCR −6.56, HELMET-ICL −13.84, RepoQA −26.50.
- Searched layers: RULER −5.69, MRCR −1.81, HELMET-ICL −2.76, RepoQA −14.66.

The authors call the alternating layout's loss "catastrophic". They say the efficient variants (the window and two linear-attention ones) all keep "an inherent accuracy gap on fine-grained retrieval tasks". So GLM-5 uses DeepSeek Sparse Attention instead, which they call lossless "by construction" ([p. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?page=7&search=DSA%20is%20lossless%20by%20construction)). Their own small test is weaker than that claim: it ends 0.35 below the baseline on RULER at 128K, after dropping from 79.21 to 71.35 at the warmup stage ([p. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?page=7&search=79.21)).

## How the findings fit together

- **The papers agree where both measure.** At 4K, where the 4096 window covers the whole input, GLM's windowed model matches full attention. That fits Gemma's perplexity result and Mistral's short-benchmark claim.
- **The cost shows up in long-range retrieval,** which only GLM-5 tests. There, which layers keep full attention matters more than how many: same 1:1 ratio, 6.51 vs 53.95 at 128K before training.
- **GLM's test is the worst case for a window.** It was added to a model trained with full attention. Gemma and Mistral trained with the window from the start, which GLM doesn't test. So GLM's numbers may overstate what a trained-in window costs, and Gemma's say nothing about it either way.

All page numbers were checked against the PDF text with `paperlib issues look`. Where the markdown headings disagreed with the PDF (Gemma Figs. 4–5 and GLM Tables 4–5), I used the PDF page. Gemma's perplexity claims rest on figures, and I read the authors' description of them, not plotted numbers. I didn't change any files, so there's nothing to commit.
